# _autosummary/inkmap.coverage.html.md

# inkmap.coverage

Per-pixel foreground coverage: the 0..1 value, and which one you want.

Three different 0..1 quantities get conflated by “how foreground is this pixel”. They
answer different questions, and mixing them produces numbers that mean nothing:

**Coverage** ([`coverage_map()`](_autosummary/inkmap.coverage.html.md#inkmap.coverage.coverage_map), [`observed_coverage()`](_autosummary/inkmap.coverage.html.md#inkmap.coverage.observed_coverage)) is *physical*: the
fraction of the pixel’s area lying under foreground. ISO 12647-2:2013 3.1 calls this
**area coverage**. A pixel straddling a mark’s edge genuinely is 0.37 foreground. The
same quantity is the matting **alpha** (identical, for opaque marks), the
remote-sensing **fractional abundance** of an endmember in a **mixed pixel**, and the
medical-imaging **partial volume fraction**.

**Confidence** ([`confidence()`](_autosummary/inkmap.coverage.html.md#inkmap.coverage.confidence)) is *epistemic*: how sure we are of the label. This
is what the user’s “probability that the pixel is foreground” means when the underlying
reality is genuinely binary. A pixel deep inside a mark has coverage 1.0 and confidence
1.0; one in a blown-out highlight may have modelled coverage 1.0 and confidence near 0.

**Weight** ([`measurement_weight()`](_autosummary/inkmap.coverage.html.md#inkmap.coverage.measurement_weight)) is *operational*: how safe the pixel is to
measure, given that blur spreads signal across boundaries. It is the only one that
should gate a physical measurement.

## Two routes to coverage

*Modelled* ([`coverage_map()`](_autosummary/inkmap.coverage.html.md#inkmap.coverage.coverage_map)): the shape is known, so back-project a supersampled
grid of each pixel through the transform and ask the model. Exact up to the
supersampling rate, immune to lighting, and the right default. It answers “where should
the foreground be”.

*Observed* ([`observed_coverage()`](_autosummary/inkmap.coverage.html.md#inkmap.coverage.observed_coverage)): normalise the photograph between a background
endpoint and a solid-foreground endpoint. This is the Murray-Davies inversion, and it
answers “where is the foreground actually” – so it is the one that can see a printing
defect. It returns an *apparent* (optical) coverage, inflated relative to geometric
coverage by lateral light scattering in the substrate (the Yule-Nielsen effect), which
is why the two routes disagree.

### Functions

| [`coverage_map`](_autosummary/inkmap.coverage.html.md#inkmap.coverage.coverage_map)(model, transform, image_shape, \*)   | Area fraction of each pixel covered by the model's foreground, in `[0, 1]`.   |
|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`observed_coverage`](_autosummary/inkmap.coverage.html.md#inkmap.coverage.observed_coverage)(gray, placement, \*[, ...])     | Apparent coverage read from the photograph itself (Murray-Davies).            |
| [`confidence`](_autosummary/inkmap.coverage.html.md#inkmap.coverage.confidence)(gray, placement, coverage, \*[, ...])  | How much to trust the coverage value at each pixel, in `[0, 1]`.              |
| [`measurement_weight`](_autosummary/inkmap.coverage.html.md#inkmap.coverage.measurement_weight)(coverage, \*[, ...])           | Blur-aware weight in `[0, 1]`: how safe each pixel is to *measure*.           |
| [`region_map`](_autosummary/inkmap.coverage.html.md#inkmap.coverage.region_map)(placement, coverage, \*[, ...])        | Four-way `Region` label array from a coverage map and a placement.            |
| [`estimate_blur_sigma`](_autosummary/inkmap.coverage.html.md#inkmap.coverage.estimate_blur_sigma)(gray, placement)              | Estimate imaging blur sigma, in pixels, from the mark's own edges.            |

### inkmap.coverage.confidence(gray, placement, coverage, , polarity=Polarity.FOREGROUND_IS_DARK)

How much to trust the coverage value at each pixel, in `[0, 1]`.

Distinct from coverage. Three things erode it, combined multiplicatively:

* **Model/image disagreement** – where the observed value contradicts the modelled
  coverage, one of them is wrong. This is what catches foreground that failed to
  print, a torn label, or a mis-fitted transform.
* **Clipping** – saturated or crushed pixels carry no photometric information.
* **Edge proximity** – mixed pixels are inherently less certain, and their value
  depends on sub-pixel geometry known only to ~0.5 px.

* **Return type:**
  `ndarray`

### inkmap.coverage.coverage_map(model, transform, image_shape, , samples=8)

Area fraction of each pixel covered by the model’s foreground, in `[0, 1]`.

Each pixel is probed at `samples**2` sub-positions on a regular grid at sub-pixel
centres; each probe is back-projected into model coordinates and passed to
`Model.occupancy()`. The mean is the covered area fraction – ordinary
supersampled area coverage, the same quantity a renderer’s anti-aliasing computes.

Values are quantised to `1/samples**2`, so `samples` sets the accuracy floor.
Only the model’s bounding box is evaluated, so a mark occupying 2% of a 12 MP photo
costs 2% of the work.

* **Return type:**
  `ndarray`

### inkmap.coverage.estimate_blur_sigma(gray, placement)

Estimate imaging blur sigma, in pixels, from the mark’s own edges.

Sizing the measurement margin needs this. Estimated by finding the sigma whose
blurred ideal coverage best matches the photograph.

Returns `nan` when the minimum lands at the top of the search range: that is the
search running out of room, not a measurement – the modelled shape and the
photograph do not correspond – and reporting the boundary value would silently size
the measurement margin from noise.

* **Return type:**
  [`float`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)

### inkmap.coverage.measurement_weight(coverage, , blur_sigma=None, radius=None, inside=None, kind='foreground', sigmas=2.0)

Blur-aware weight in `[0, 1]`: how safe each pixel is to *measure*.

Coverage says a pixel lies entirely under foreground. That is necessary but not
sufficient: the point spread function leaks neighbouring signal into interior
pixels, and that contamination has a different footprint from partial area
coverage – so no coverage-based weighting removes it. The fix is spatial: require
a pixel’s whole neighbourhood to be foreground, out to the radius the blur reaches.

Implemented as grayscale morphological erosion of the coverage map, which is exactly
“the minimum coverage within radius r” – continuous rather than a hard mask, so a
pixel one step from an edge is down-weighted rather than trusted or discarded.

Give either `radius` (pixels, wins if both are given) or `blur_sigma`, from
which the radius is `sigmas * blur_sigma`.

* **Return type:**
  `ndarray`

### inkmap.coverage.observed_coverage(gray, placement, , polarity=Polarity.FOREGROUND_IS_DARK, yule_nielsen_n=1.0, percentile=5.0)

Apparent coverage read from the photograph itself (Murray-Davies).

Endmember values are estimated from the mark’s own pixels – its background region
gives the substrate endpoint, its foreground core the solid endpoint – so no
external calibration target is needed. Percentiles rather than extremes, so a
specular highlight cannot define an endpoint.

`yule_nielsen_n` > 1 compensates for lateral light scattering in the substrate,
which otherwise inflates apparent coverage above geometric coverage. n = 1 is plain
Murray-Davies; the right value is substrate- and wavelength-specific and should be
fitted, not guessed.

The result is *apparent*, not geometric, coverage. Do not silently substitute it
for [`coverage_map()`](_autosummary/inkmap.coverage.html.md#inkmap.coverage.coverage_map).

* **Return type:**
  `ndarray`

### inkmap.coverage.region_map(placement, coverage, , threshold=0.5, margin_units=4.0)

Four-way `Region` label array from a coverage map and a placement.

* **Return type:**
  `ndarray`


# _autosummary/inkmap.geometry.html.md

# inkmap.geometry

Model space <-> image space: transforms, and refining them against the photograph.

The central object is a homography mapping *model coordinates* to image pixels. Get it
right and every mask, sample and margin polygon follows exactly. Get it wrong by a
pixel and every downstream number inherits the error, while the mask still looks
plausible.

Three half-pixel conventions have to agree, and each is invisible on inspection:

1. **Pixel centre vs pixel corner.** OpenCV treats integer coordinate `x` as the
   *centre* of a pixel spanning `[x-0.5, x+0.5)`. Rasterising `[x, x+1)` instead –
   the natural array-indexing reading – offsets the entire coverage map by half a
   pixel.
2. **The template raster.** A model rendered at `s` px per unit puts template pixel
   `t` over `[t/s, (t+1)/s)` in model units, so its *centre* is `(t+0.5)/s`.
   Omitting that half-pixel puts a fixed ~0.7 px bias into every refinement.
3. **Detector corner conventions differ.** OpenCV’s QR corners are the integer index of
   the last *contained* pixel; zxing-cpp returns the continuous outer boundary. Measured
   directly, not read from docs – hence `inclusive_pixel_corners`.

A symptom worth recognising: if refinement error grows with the mark’s rotation angle
in the pattern `R(d) - d`, the residual `d` is a coordinate-convention offset, not
noise.

### Functions

| [`model_quad`](_autosummary/inkmap.geometry.html.md#inkmap.geometry.model_quad)(model)                            | The model's four extent corners in model coordinates, top-left first.     |
|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`quad_to_transform`](_autosummary/inkmap.geometry.html.md#inkmap.geometry.quad_to_transform)(quad, model, \*[, ...])    | Homography mapping model coordinates onto an image quad.                  |
| [`transform_to_quad`](_autosummary/inkmap.geometry.html.md#inkmap.geometry.transform_to_quad)(transform, model)          | Image-space corners implied by a transform, in model order.               |
| [`pixels_per_unit`](_autosummary/inkmap.geometry.html.md#inkmap.geometry.pixels_per_unit)(transform, model)            | Mean image pixels per model unit implied by a transform.                  |
| [`refine_transform`](_autosummary/inkmap.geometry.html.md#inkmap.geometry.refine_transform)(gray, model, transform, \*) | Refine a model->image transform by ECC-aligning the rendered model.       |
| [`margin_quad`](_autosummary/inkmap.geometry.html.md#inkmap.geometry.margin_quad)(transform, model, \*[, units])   | Image-space quad of the model plus a clear margin of `units` model units. |
| [`cell_centers`](_autosummary/inkmap.geometry.html.md#inkmap.geometry.cell_centers)(transform, n_cols, n_rows)      | `(n_rows, n_cols, 2)` image coordinates of unit-cell centres.             |

### inkmap.geometry.cell_centers(transform, n_cols, n_rows)

`(n_rows, n_cols, 2)` image coordinates of unit-cell centres.

Meaningful for grid models. ISO/IEC 18004’s reference decode algorithm samples a
small area at each grid intersection – deliberately avoiding edges rather than
modelling them – and this is where to do the same.

* **Return type:**
  `ndarray`

### inkmap.geometry.margin_quad(transform, model, , units=4.0)

Image-space quad of the model plus a clear margin of `units` model units.

ISO/IEC 18004 mandates a 4-module quiet zone for QR; linear symbologies specify
light margins; printed text has its own whitespace. The margin is guaranteed
background, which makes it a reference region that – unlike background *inside*
the mark – carries no risk of spread from adjacent foreground.

* **Return type:**
  `ndarray`

### inkmap.geometry.model_quad(model)

The model’s four extent corners in model coordinates, top-left first.

* **Return type:**
  `ndarray`

### inkmap.geometry.pixels_per_unit(transform, model)

Mean image pixels per model unit implied by a transform.

* **Return type:**
  [`float`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)

### inkmap.geometry.quad_to_transform(quad, model, , inclusive_pixel_corners=False)

Homography mapping model coordinates onto an image quad.

`quad` must be in the *model’s* own corner order (its top-left first), which is
what the locators natively produce – do not re-sort it.

Set `inclusive_pixel_corners=True` for detectors whose corners are the integer
index of the last contained pixel rather than the continuous outer edge. The quad
is then expanded half a pixel outward, removing a systematic one-pixel scale error
– which is a third of a unit at 3 px per unit.

* **Return type:**
  `ndarray`

### inkmap.geometry.refine_transform(gray, model, transform, , iterations=200, eps=1e-07, blur_frac=0.25, min_correlation=0.5, margin_units=2.0)

Refine a model->image transform by ECC-aligning the rendered model.

Four detector corners are four observations; the model’s whole shape is thousands.
Aligning the rendered pattern therefore pins the 8-DoF homography far more tightly
– measured at 0.02-0.03 px corner RMS versus ~1 px from detector corners.

Returns `(transform, correlation)`, falling back to the input unchanged when the
optimiser fails or the correlation lands below `min_correlation` – a refinement
that did not converge is worse than none.

Two details do most of the work. The template is rendered at the *observed* scale;
rendering at a fixed small scale aliases the comparison and makes the result
measurably worse than no refinement at all. And the template carries a clear margin,
because blurring a template that stops at the mark’s edge makes the kernel reflect
interior content back across the border, inventing an edge profile the photograph
does not have – ECC then shifts the whole fit to match the artefact.

* **Return type:**
  [`tuple`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#tuple)[`ndarray`, [`float`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)]

### inkmap.geometry.transform_to_quad(transform, model)

Image-space corners implied by a transform, in model order.

* **Return type:**
  `ndarray`


# _autosummary/inkmap.html.md

# inkmap

inkmap – per-pixel foreground coverage for photographed marks.

Given a photograph of a printed mark and a *model* of its shape, say for every pixel
how much of it is foreground (the mark) and how much is background (the substrate) –
as a continuous fraction, not a boolean.

The model is the seam. QR symbols, barcodes, printed letters and arbitrary artwork all
go through one pipeline, because all a model has to do is answer “is this point, in my
own coordinate system, foreground?”:

```default
import inkmap
from inkmap import models

inkmap.find(photo)                                        # auto-detect QR/barcode
inkmap.find(photo, model=models.text_model("ABC"), quad=q)  # a printed word
inkmap.find(photo, model=models.RasterModel(art), quad=q)   # anything you can draw
```

The simplest call:

```default
coverage = inkmap.foreground(photo)   # (H, W) float32 in [0, 1]
```

With geometry:

```default
ink = inkmap.find(photo)              # an InkMap, or None
ink.placement.quad                    # (4, 2) corners -- a quadrilateral, not a
                                      # rectangle: perspective is expected
ink.coverage                          # (H, W) float32 area coverage
ink.region                            # OUTSIDE / MARGIN / BACKGROUND / FOREGROUND
ink.weight                            # (H, W) float32 safe-to-measure weighting
```

Measuring:

```default
mask = inkmap.measurement_mask(ink)   # pure pixels, eroded clear of edges
result = inkmap.measure(photo, ink)
result.contrast                       # foreground minus background, linearised
result.measurability.ok               # False if the image cannot support this
```

## Terminology

The two classes are **foreground** and **background**, never dark and light: dark/light
describe appearance, and appearance inverts (white-on-black print, reflectance-reversed
symbols, inverted imaging), so an appearance name would mean the mark in one image and
the substrate in the next. [`Polarity`](_autosummary/inkmap.html.md#inkmap.Polarity) carries that mapping explicitly. The
continuous value is **coverage**, after ISO 12647-2:2013 3.1 *area coverage*. See
`docs/terminology.md`.

### Functions

| [`foreground`](_autosummary/inkmap.html.md#inkmap.foreground)(image, \*\*kwargs)                      | Foreground coverage of the largest mark, `(H, W) float32` in `[0, 1]`.         |
|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`find`](_autosummary/inkmap.html.md#inkmap.find)(image, \*\*kwargs)                            | The largest mark in `image`, or `None`.                                        |
| [`find_all`](_autosummary/inkmap.html.md#inkmap.find_all)(image, \*[, model, quad, locators, ...])  | Find every mark in `image` and compute its foreground coverage.                |
| [`place`](_autosummary/inkmap.html.md#inkmap.place)(model, quad, \*[, ...])                      | Place a model at a known quadrilateral -- the universal escape hatch.          |
| [`measure`](_autosummary/inkmap.html.md#inkmap.measure)(image, ink_map, \*[, linearize, ...])      | Aggregate `image` over the safe foreground and background pixels of `ink_map`. |
| [`measurement_mask`](_autosummary/inkmap.html.md#inkmap.measurement_mask)(ink_map, \*[, kind, purity, ...]) | Pixels safe to measure: geometrically pure, then eroded clear of edges.        |
| [`measurability`](_autosummary/inkmap.html.md#inkmap.measurability)(ink_map, \*[, min_pixels])           | Judge whether a foreground/background measurement can be trusted here.         |
| [`srgb_to_linear`](_autosummary/inkmap.html.md#inkmap.srgb_to_linear)(image)                              | Undo the sRGB transfer function, returning float in `[0, 1]`.                  |
| [`coverage_map`](_autosummary/inkmap.html.md#inkmap.coverage_map)(model, transform, image_shape, \*)    | Area fraction of each pixel covered by the model's foreground, in `[0, 1]`.    |
| [`observed_coverage`](_autosummary/inkmap.html.md#inkmap.observed_coverage)(gray, placement, \*[, ...])      | Apparent coverage read from the photograph itself (Murray-Davies).             |
| [`confidence`](_autosummary/inkmap.html.md#inkmap.confidence)(gray, placement, coverage, \*[, ...])   | How much to trust the coverage value at each pixel, in `[0, 1]`.               |
| [`measurement_weight`](_autosummary/inkmap.html.md#inkmap.measurement_weight)(coverage, \*[, ...])            | Blur-aware weight in `[0, 1]`: how safe each pixel is to *measure*.            |
| [`locate`](_autosummary/inkmap.html.md#inkmap.locate)(bgr, gray, \*[, locators, first_hit, ...])  | Run locator strategies and merge their results, de-duplicating by position.    |
| [`find_square_marks`](_autosummary/inkmap.html.md#inkmap.find_square_marks)(gray, \*[, min_side_px, ...])    | Every solid or nested square mark in `gray` (2-D, 0-255 scale), largest first. |

### Classes

| [`InkMap`](_autosummary/inkmap.html.md#inkmap.InkMap)(coverage, region, placement[, ...])        | Per-pixel foreground coverage for one placement, plus the geometry it came from.   |
|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`Placement`](_autosummary/inkmap.html.md#inkmap.Placement)(model, transform, quad[, locator, ...]) | A located instance of a model: which shape, and where it sits in the image.        |
| [`Region`](_autosummary/inkmap.html.md#inkmap.Region)(\*values)                                  | Four-way pixel classification.                                                     |
| [`Polarity`](_autosummary/inkmap.html.md#inkmap.Polarity)(\*values)                                | Which apparent-brightness state the foreground corresponds to.                     |
| [`Model`](_autosummary/inkmap.html.md#inkmap.Model)(\*args, \*\*kwargs)                         | The shape of a mark, in its own coordinate system.                                 |
| [`Measurement`](_autosummary/inkmap.html.md#inkmap.Measurement)(foreground_mean, foreground_std, ...) | Aggregated signal over foreground and background, with its validity attached.      |
| [`Measurability`](_autosummary/inkmap.html.md#inkmap.Measurability)(ok, pixels_per_feature, ...[, ...]) | Whether a trustworthy measurement is possible on this image at all.                |
| [`SquareMark`](_autosummary/inkmap.html.md#inkmap.SquareMark)(centre, corners, side_px[, ...])       | One square mark found in an image.                                                 |

### *class* inkmap.InkMap(coverage, region, placement, polarity=Polarity.FOREGROUND_IS_DARK, weight=None, blur_sigma=None, metadata=dict())

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

Per-pixel foreground coverage for one placement, plus the geometry it came from.

`coverage` is *geometric* area coverage: the fraction of each pixel’s area lying
under foreground. It is not an optical/reflectance-derived coverage (which lateral
light scattering in the substrate inflates – the Murray-Davies/Yule-Nielsen
effect), and it is not a probability. See [`confidence()`](_autosummary/inkmap.html.md#inkmap.confidence) for that.

#### background_mask(, threshold=0.5)

Bare-substrate pixels within the mark’s footprint (not the margin).

* **Return type:**
  `ndarray`

#### blur_sigma *: [float](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float) | [None](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/constants.html#None)* *= None*

Estimated image blur (px). `nan` means estimation failed – typically because
the modelled shape and the photograph do not correspond.

#### coverage *: ndarray*

(H, W) float32 in [0, 1]. Zero outside the mark.

#### foreground_mask(, threshold=0.5)

Boolean foreground mask by thresholding coverage. Fine for display and
labelling; for anything photometric use [`inkmap.measurement_mask()`](_autosummary/inkmap.html.md#inkmap.measurement_mask)
instead, which accounts for blur.

* **Return type:**
  `ndarray`

#### inside_mask(, margin=False)

Every pixel within the mark’s footprint. With `margin=True`, include the
clear surround as well.

* **Return type:**
  `ndarray`

#### margin_mask()

The clear surround – an alternative reference region.

* **Return type:**
  `ndarray`

#### region *: ndarray*

(H, W) uint8 of [`Region`](_autosummary/inkmap.html.md#inkmap.Region) values.

#### weight *: ndarray | [None](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/constants.html#None)* *= None*

(H, W) float32 in [0, 1] – the blur-aware measurement weight, and the **only**
channel that should gate a physical measurement. Coverage is geometric and ignores
the point spread function; confidence is epistemic and says nothing about
partial-area contamination. See [`inkmap.coverage.measurement_weight()`](_autosummary/inkmap.coverage.html.md#inkmap.coverage.measurement_weight).

### *class* inkmap.Measurability(ok, pixels_per_feature, blur_sigma, resolution_ratio, n_foreground_pixels, n_background_pixels, reasons=())

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

Whether a trustworthy measurement is possible on this image at all.

#### resolution_ratio *: [float](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)*

`pixels_per_feature / blur_sigma`. Below ~6 the blur is wide relative to the
mark’s smallest feature and no erosion leaves uncontaminated pixels.

### *class* inkmap.Measurement(foreground_mean, foreground_std, foreground_median, background_mean, background_std, background_median, n_foreground, n_background, measurability=None, metadata=dict())

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

Aggregated signal over foreground and background, with its validity attached.

`measurability` is carried along deliberately: a caller that ignores it has to do
so explicitly.

#### *property* contrast *: [float](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)*

Foreground minus background.

#### *property* ratio *: [float](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)*

Foreground over background; `nan` when the background reads zero.

#### *property* snr *: [float](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)*

Contrast over the pooled standard deviation.

### *class* inkmap.Model(\*args, \*\*kwargs)

Bases: [`Protocol`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Protocol)

The shape of a mark, in its own coordinate system.

Implement this – or just duck-type it – to teach the package a new kind of mark.
Two members are required; `render()` has a working default in
`BaseModel`.

#### *property* extent *: [tuple](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#tuple)[[float](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float), [float](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)]*

`(width, height)` of model space, in the model’s natural units.

#### *property* feature_size *: [float](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)*

Size of the smallest feature that must be resolved, in model units.

A model unit is not a feature. A QR module *is* the smallest feature, so its
feature size is 1. But a glyph rendered onto a 512-cell raster has strokes tens
of cells wide, and a model unit there is far smaller than anything that must be
resolved. Whether an image can support a measurement depends on pixels per
*feature*, not pixels per unit, so this is what makes that judgement portable
across model kinds.

`BaseModel` estimates it from the rendered shape; grid models override
it with the exact value.

#### occupancy(u, v)

Foreground indicator at model coordinates `(u, v)`.

`u` and `v` are float arrays of any matching shape. Returns an array of the
same shape, boolean or float in `[0, 1]`. Points outside [`extent`](_autosummary/inkmap.html.md#inkmap.Model.extent) must
return 0 – callers rely on that to bound the mark.

Must be vectorised: it is called with millions of points.

* **Return type:**
  `ndarray`

### *class* inkmap.Placement(model, transform, quad, locator='', payload=None, refined=False, score=None, metadata=dict())

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

A located instance of a model: which shape, and where it sits in the image.

`transform` is the bridge the whole package is built on – a 3x3 homography from
*model space* (the model’s own units, origin at its top-left) to image pixels. The
quad is just its image under that transform, kept for convenience.

#### locator *: [str](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)* *= ''*

Which locator strategy produced this.

#### payload *: [str](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str) | [None](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/constants.html#None)* *= None*

Decoded content, when the locator happened to decode something. Never required:
decoding is not the point, and a barely-deposited mark may locate but not decode.

#### *property* pixels_per_feature *: [float](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)*

Image pixels across the model’s smallest feature.

**This** is the resolution figure that governs whether a trustworthy
measurement is possible – not [`pixels_per_unit`](_autosummary/inkmap.html.md#inkmap.Placement.pixels_per_unit). A model unit is not a
feature: a QR module is both, but a glyph rendered onto a 512-cell raster has
strokes tens of cells wide, so pixels-per-unit there would understate the real
resolution by that factor and declare every image unmeasurable.

#### *property* pixels_per_unit *: [float](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)*

Image pixels per model unit.

For a QR symbol a “unit” is one module; for a barcode, one narrow bar; for a
raster model, one raster cell. Use [`pixels_per_feature`](_autosummary/inkmap.html.md#inkmap.Placement.pixels_per_feature) to reason about
whether the image resolves the mark.

#### quad *: ndarray*

(4, 2) float32 image-space corners of the model’s extent, in the *model’s* own
order (its top-left first), not re-sorted into image order. Re-sorting by
coordinate sum/difference – a common idiom – silently mislabels corners once the
mark is rotated past 45 degrees, which rotates the model and corrupts every derived
mask while leaving it looking plausible.

#### score *: [float](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float) | [None](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/constants.html#None)* *= None*

Alignment score from refinement, if it ran. A proxy for geometric fit quality.

#### transform *: ndarray*

(3, 3) float64, model coordinates -> image pixels.

#### *property* units_per_pixel *: [float](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)*

Model units spanned by one image pixel, averaged over the two axes.

### *class* inkmap.Polarity(\*values)

Bases: [`IntEnum`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/enum.html#enum.IntEnum)

Which apparent-brightness state the foreground corresponds to.

Carried explicitly so that no appearance word ever has to stand in for a physical
class. Flipping this is the supported way to handle inverted print and inverted
imaging, rather than inverting masks at the call site.

#### FOREGROUND_IS_DARK *= 0*

ink absorbs, so the mark reads darker than the substrate.

* **Type:**
  The usual case

#### FOREGROUND_IS_LIGHT *= 1*

the mark reads brighter than the substrate.

* **Type:**
  Reversed

### *class* inkmap.Region(\*values)

Bases: [`IntEnum`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/enum.html#enum.IntEnum)

Four-way pixel classification.

Not a matting *trimap*: a trimap’s third class is “unknown/undecided”, whereas
every class here is a decided statement about location.

#### BACKGROUND *= 2*

Bare substrate within the mark’s footprint.

#### FOREGROUND *= 3*

The mark itself – printed ink, toner, engraving, whatever laid it down.

#### MARGIN *= 1*

The clear surround a mark is specified to have – a QR quiet zone, a barcode
light margin, the whitespace around a glyph. Guaranteed background, contiguous, and
free of edge effects from neighbouring foreground, which often makes it a better
reference region than the background *inside* the mark.

#### OUTSIDE *= 0*

Outside the mark and its margin.

### *class* inkmap.SquareMark(centre, corners, side_px, rings=(), sigma_px=nan, centres=())

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

One square mark found in an image. Coordinates are pixels, `(x, y)`.

`corners` are the outer square’s, clockwise as seen on screen, starting from the
one nearest the image’s top-left. A square has no intrinsic first corner, so that
order is a convention, not an identification. `rings` is the side of each nested
square as a fraction of the outer one, outermost first (empty for a solid mark).
`centres` are the outer square’s centre followed by each nested square’s, each
where that square’s diagonals cross; `centre` is their mean weighted by side,
which for a solid mark is the outer square’s own.

#### ring_error(expected)

Largest difference between these ring ratios and `expected`; inf if unlike.

```pycon
>>> SquareMark((0, 0), np.zeros((4, 2)), 10.0, rings=(0.7, 0.4)).ring_error(
...     QR_FINDER_RINGS
... )
0.028...
>>> SquareMark((0, 0), np.zeros((4, 2)), 10.0).ring_error(BULLSEYE_RINGS)
inf
```

* **Return type:**
  [`float`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)

### inkmap.confidence(gray, placement, coverage, , polarity=Polarity.FOREGROUND_IS_DARK)

How much to trust the coverage value at each pixel, in `[0, 1]`.

Distinct from coverage. Three things erode it, combined multiplicatively:

* **Model/image disagreement** – where the observed value contradicts the modelled
  coverage, one of them is wrong. This is what catches foreground that failed to
  print, a torn label, or a mis-fitted transform.
* **Clipping** – saturated or crushed pixels carry no photometric information.
* **Edge proximity** – mixed pixels are inherently less certain, and their value
  depends on sub-pixel geometry known only to ~0.5 px.

* **Return type:**
  `ndarray`

### inkmap.coverage_map(model, transform, image_shape, , samples=8)

Area fraction of each pixel covered by the model’s foreground, in `[0, 1]`.

Each pixel is probed at `samples**2` sub-positions on a regular grid at sub-pixel
centres; each probe is back-projected into model coordinates and passed to
[`Model.occupancy()`](_autosummary/inkmap.html.md#inkmap.Model.occupancy). The mean is the covered area fraction – ordinary
supersampled area coverage, the same quantity a renderer’s anti-aliasing computes.

Values are quantised to `1/samples**2`, so `samples` sets the accuracy floor.
Only the model’s bounding box is evaluated, so a mark occupying 2% of a 12 MP photo
costs 2% of the work.

* **Return type:**
  `ndarray`

### inkmap.find(image, \*\*kwargs)

The largest mark in `image`, or `None`. See [`find_all()`](_autosummary/inkmap.html.md#inkmap.find_all).

* **Return type:**
  [`InkMap`](_autosummary/inkmap.types.html.md#inkmap.types.InkMap) | [`None`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/constants.html#None)

### inkmap.find_all(image, , model=None, quad=None, locators=('qr_zxing', 'qr_aruco', 'qr_opencv', 'barcode_zxing'), locate_scale=None, \*\*kwargs)

Find every mark in `image` and compute its foreground coverage.

With `model` and `quad`, skips detection entirely and analyses that one
placement – the path for marks no detector knows about. With neither, runs the
locator cascade (QR and linear barcodes out of the box).

`refine` (default on) aligns the rendered model to the photograph, pinning the
transform to sub-pixel accuracy; it is far more accurate than locator corners alone
and costs a few milliseconds.

`source` picks where coverage comes from: `"modelled"` (default) computes it
from the model – exact and lighting-independent, answering “where should the
foreground be”. `"observed"` reads it from the photograph, answering “where is
the foreground actually”, and so is the one that can see a printing defect.

`locate_scale` (e.g. `0.5`) locates on a downscaled copy of the frame and maps
the placements back – several times faster on large photographs, with refinement
restoring sub-pixel geometry. Codes need about 4 px per module *after* downscaling
(`config.MIN_COARSE_PIXELS_PER_FEATURE`); those below are re-located at full
resolution. `None` (default) locates at full resolution. See
[`inkmap.locate()`](_autosummary/inkmap.html.md#inkmap.locate) (its `scale`). Ignored when `model`/`quad` are given.

* **Return type:**
  [`list`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#list)[[`InkMap`](_autosummary/inkmap.types.html.md#inkmap.types.InkMap)]

### inkmap.find_square_marks(gray, , min_side_px=8.0, max_side_share=0.1, polarity=Polarity.FOREGROUND_IS_DARK, dark_share=0.72, min_contrast=6.0, local_window_share=0.12)

Every solid or nested square mark in `gray` (2-D, 0-255 scale), largest first.

A mark’s outer square must be at least `min_side_px` on a side and at most
`max_side_share` of the frame’s shorter side. Nested marks report their ring
ratios; solid marks report none. `polarity` says whether the marks read darker
than the substrate (the usual case) or brighter.

The foreground is binarised relative to the local mean brightness: a pixel is
foreground when it is darker than `dark_share` of the mean over a window
`local_window_share` of the frame’s shorter side, and darker by at least
`min_contrast` grey levels. The window is widened to stay wider than the largest
mark looked for, since a mark wider than it is hollowed by its own ink.

Anything square is a candidate: a QR symbol’s clusters of data modules and some
printed glyphs come back as solid marks too. Telling the registration marks from
them, by size, ring ratio and layout, is the caller’s.

* **Return type:**
  [`list`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#list)[[`SquareMark`](_autosummary/inkmap.html.md#inkmap.SquareMark)]

### inkmap.foreground(image, \*\*kwargs)

Foreground coverage of the largest mark, `(H, W) float32` in `[0, 1]`.

All-zero if nothing is found – the one-liner never raises on a miss, so it can be
mapped over a directory. Use [`find()`](_autosummary/inkmap.html.md#inkmap.find) to tell “no mark” from “a mark with no
foreground”.

* **Return type:**
  `ndarray`

### inkmap.locate(bgr, gray, , locators=('qr_zxing', 'qr_aruco', 'qr_opencv', 'barcode_zxing'), first_hit=False, scale=None, full_res_retry=True)

Run locator strategies and merge their results, de-duplicating by position.

Strategies are tried in order. With `first_hit=True` the cascade stops at the
first strategy that finds anything – cheaper, and usually right when you know there
is one mark. Otherwise every strategy runs and results merge, which is what earns
the recall when an image holds several marks that no single detector finds all of.

**Coarse-to-fine.** `scale` (`0 < scale <= 1`) runs the cascade on a copy of the
frame downscaled by that factor (`cv2.INTER_AREA`), then maps every placement back
to full-resolution pixels. Locating costs roughly in proportion to pixel count, so
on a 4000 x 3000 photograph 0.5 is about 4x faster and 0.35 about 7x. `None` (the
default) or `1` locate at full resolution, exactly as without the argument.

Every locator – a registered name or your own callable – is handed the
*downscaled* `bgr` and `gray` (and, on a retry, a full-resolution crop), and
must return placements in the coordinates of the frame it was given; mapping them
back to the full frame is done here. A locator that bakes in absolute pixel sizes
or positions will misbehave under `scale`.

The mapping is one affine `A` (small -> full pixels), in the pixel-centre
convention `cv2.resize` uses, `x_full = (x_small + 0.5) / scale - 0.5`, applied
to both `quad` and `transform` (`A @ transform`). Locator name and payload are
kept; `metadata["locate_scale"]` records the scale used. Corner conventions differ
by locator (OpenCV’s are inclusive pixel indices, zxing’s are the continuous outer
boundary), so a locator’s own half-pixel bias is magnified by `1 / scale` on the
way up – a pixel or so at 0.5. That does not matter downstream when
`inkmap.analyze()` refines (its default), which pins the transform to sub-pixel
accuracy at full resolution anyway.

**The model is the fragile part, not the geometry.** Locators read the model off
the frame they are given – a QR’s module count and module matrix, a barcode’s bar
pattern – and refinement cannot repair a wrong model, it only fits its geometry.
Below about `config.MIN_COARSE_PIXELS_PER_FEATURE` (4) pixels per module in the
downscaled frame those reads go wrong while the code still decodes: a 25 x 25 QR
read as 21 x 21, or tens of flipped modules. So, with `full_res_retry` (default
on; only meaningful with `scale < 1`), a coarse placement is re-located on a
padded full-resolution crop around it when either its `payload` is `None` (found
but not decoded – typically a small, far-away code) or its pixels per feature in
the downscaled frame are under that floor. The full-resolution result replaces it
(`metadata["locate_retry"]` names the reason, `"undecoded"` or
`"undersampled"`, and `locate_scale` becomes 1.0). Crops are small, so this
costs little; pick `scale` so your codes clear the floor (at 0.5, 8 px per module
at full resolution) and it never triggers. A coarse placement under the floor that
is kept anyway – `full_res_retry=False`, or the crop found nothing – carries
`metadata["locate_undersampled"] = True`: treat its model as unreliable. A mark
the coarse pass misses entirely is not recovered: lower the downscaling instead.

* **Return type:**
  [`list`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#list)[[`Placement`](_autosummary/inkmap.types.html.md#inkmap.types.Placement)]

### inkmap.measurability(ink_map, , min_pixels=50)

Judge whether a foreground/background measurement can be trusted here.

Returning a number quietly biased by 30% is worse than refusing, so this is checked
up front and attached to every [`Measurement`](_autosummary/inkmap.html.md#inkmap.Measurement).

* **Return type:**
  [`Measurability`](_autosummary/inkmap.photometry.html.md#inkmap.photometry.Measurability)

### inkmap.measure(image, ink_map, , linearize=True, flatten=False, margin=None, robust=True)

Aggregate `image` over the safe foreground and background pixels of `ink_map`.

`image` need not be the one the mark was located in: any frame registered to it
works, which is the usual way to measure a different exposure, channel or modality
using geometry established once on the sharpest frame.

`linearize` undoes sRGB encoding first – leave it on for anything from a normal
camera pipeline, off for already-linear data. `flatten` divides out a fitted
illumination field. `robust` reports medians alongside means; on real photographs
they diverge exactly where something is wrong, which makes the pair a free
diagnostic.

* **Return type:**
  [`Measurement`](_autosummary/inkmap.photometry.html.md#inkmap.photometry.Measurement)

### inkmap.measurement_mask(ink_map, , kind='foreground', purity=0.999, margin=None)

Pixels safe to measure: geometrically pure, then eroded clear of edges.

`kind` selects `"foreground"` or `"background"`. `purity` is the coverage
threshold for “pure”; the default demands essentially total coverage, which is the
point – a partially covered pixel biases the mean toward the other class.

This is the mask to use for a measurement. [`InkMap.foreground_mask()`](_autosummary/inkmap.html.md#inkmap.InkMap.foreground_mask) is for
display and for anything that only needs a label.

* **Return type:**
  `ndarray`

### inkmap.measurement_weight(coverage, , blur_sigma=None, radius=None, inside=None, kind='foreground', sigmas=2.0)

Blur-aware weight in `[0, 1]`: how safe each pixel is to *measure*.

Coverage says a pixel lies entirely under foreground. That is necessary but not
sufficient: the point spread function leaks neighbouring signal into interior
pixels, and that contamination has a different footprint from partial area
coverage – so no coverage-based weighting removes it. The fix is spatial: require
a pixel’s whole neighbourhood to be foreground, out to the radius the blur reaches.

Implemented as grayscale morphological erosion of the coverage map, which is exactly
“the minimum coverage within radius r” – continuous rather than a hard mask, so a
pixel one step from an edge is down-weighted rather than trusted or discarded.

Give either `radius` (pixels, wins if both are given) or `blur_sigma`, from
which the radius is `sigmas * blur_sigma`.

* **Return type:**
  `ndarray`

### inkmap.observed_coverage(gray, placement, , polarity=Polarity.FOREGROUND_IS_DARK, yule_nielsen_n=1.0, percentile=5.0)

Apparent coverage read from the photograph itself (Murray-Davies).

Endmember values are estimated from the mark’s own pixels – its background region
gives the substrate endpoint, its foreground core the solid endpoint – so no
external calibration target is needed. Percentiles rather than extremes, so a
specular highlight cannot define an endpoint.

`yule_nielsen_n` > 1 compensates for lateral light scattering in the substrate,
which otherwise inflates apparent coverage above geometric coverage. n = 1 is plain
Murray-Davies; the right value is substrate- and wavelength-specific and should be
fitted, not guessed.

The result is *apparent*, not geometric, coverage. Do not silently substitute it
for [`coverage_map()`](_autosummary/inkmap.html.md#inkmap.coverage_map).

* **Return type:**
  `ndarray`

### inkmap.place(model, quad, , inclusive_pixel_corners=False, locator='manual', \*\*metadata)

Place a model at a known quadrilateral – the universal escape hatch.

`quad` is four `(x, y)` image points in the *model’s* own corner order: the
point corresponding to model-space `(0, 0)` first, then clockwise. Order matters
and is not inferred: sorting corners by image position silently mislabels them once
the mark is rotated past 45 degrees.

Use this for anything without a decoder – printed letters, logos, engraved marks –
or when you already know where the mark is and only want the coverage machinery.

* **Return type:**
  [`Placement`](_autosummary/inkmap.types.html.md#inkmap.types.Placement)

### inkmap.srgb_to_linear(image)

Undo the sRGB transfer function, returning float in `[0, 1]`.

Averaging pixel values without this is a real error, not a nicety: sRGB values are
perceptually encoded, so the mean of encoded values is not the encoded mean
intensity. Any difference between two exposures compounds it. Apply before any
arithmetic that claims to be about light.

The piecewise IEC 61966-2-1 curve, not the 2.2 power approximation.

* **Return type:**
  `ndarray`

# _autosummary/inkmap.models.base.html.md

# inkmap.models.base

What a *model* is, and how it becomes pixels.

A model answers one question: \*\*given a point in the mark’s own coordinate system, is
that point foreground?\*\* Everything else in this package – locating, refining,
rasterising, measuring – is written against that one question, which is why the same
machinery serves QR symbols, barcodes, printed letters and any shape a user supplies.

## Model space

Each model defines its own natural units and its own extent. A QR symbol is `N x N`
modules; a Code 128 barcode is `n x 1` modules wide by one unit tall; a glyph is
whatever its em-box says. Nothing outside this module needs to know which – the
[`Placement`](_autosummary/inkmap.types.html.md#inkmap.types.Placement) carries a homography from model space to image pixels,
and that is the only bridge required.

## Why `occupancy` and not “give me a bitmap”

Coverage is computed by supersampling each image pixel’s footprint back into model
space. If a model can answer occupancy *analytically* – and a QR module grid or a
barcode can – the result is exact, limited only by the supersampling rate. Forcing
every model through a bitmap would quantise it twice: once rendering, once sampling.
Models that genuinely are rasters (a scanned logo, a rendered glyph) implement
occupancy as a lookup and lose nothing.

### Functions

| [`render_model`](_autosummary/inkmap.models.base.html.md#inkmap.models.base.render_model)(model[, scale, supersample])   | Rasterise any model to a float `[0, 1]` array at `scale` px per model unit.   |
|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------|

### Classes

| [`Model`](_autosummary/inkmap.models.base.html.md#inkmap.models.base.Model)(\*args, \*\*kwargs)   | The shape of a mark, in its own coordinate system.        |
|------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------|
| [`BaseModel`](_autosummary/inkmap.models.base.html.md#inkmap.models.base.BaseModel)()                 | Mixin supplying `render()` and a `feature_size` estimate. |

### *class* inkmap.models.base.BaseModel

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

Mixin supplying [`render()`](_autosummary/inkmap.models.base.html.md#inkmap.models.base.BaseModel.render) and a [`feature_size`](_autosummary/inkmap.models.base.html.md#inkmap.models.base.BaseModel.feature_size) estimate.

Anything with `extent` and `occupancy` gets both for free.

#### *property* feature_size *: [float](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)*

Estimated smallest-feature size, in model units, from the rendered shape.

Taken as twice the median distance-to-edge over foreground – i.e. the typical
stroke width. The median rather than the minimum, because every shape has a few
pixels at a corner or a serif whose distance-to-edge is near zero, and letting
those set the scale would declare every image unmeasurable.

Cached: it costs a render, and the answer cannot change for an immutable model.

#### render(scale=8.0, , supersample=4)

Rasterise the model at `scale` pixels per model unit.

Returns a float array in `[0, 1]` where 1 is foreground. Anti-aliased by
supersampling, because the main consumer is template alignment against a
photograph, and a hard-edged template correlates poorly with soft real edges.

* **Return type:**
  `ndarray`

### *class* inkmap.models.base.Model(\*args, \*\*kwargs)

Bases: [`Protocol`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Protocol)

The shape of a mark, in its own coordinate system.

Implement this – or just duck-type it – to teach the package a new kind of mark.
Two members are required; `render()` has a working default in
[`BaseModel`](_autosummary/inkmap.models.base.html.md#inkmap.models.base.BaseModel).

#### *property* extent *: [tuple](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#tuple)[[float](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float), [float](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)]*

`(width, height)` of model space, in the model’s natural units.

#### *property* feature_size *: [float](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)*

Size of the smallest feature that must be resolved, in model units.

A model unit is not a feature. A QR module *is* the smallest feature, so its
feature size is 1. But a glyph rendered onto a 512-cell raster has strokes tens
of cells wide, and a model unit there is far smaller than anything that must be
resolved. Whether an image can support a measurement depends on pixels per
*feature*, not pixels per unit, so this is what makes that judgement portable
across model kinds.

[`BaseModel`](_autosummary/inkmap.models.base.html.md#inkmap.models.base.BaseModel) estimates it from the rendered shape; grid models override
it with the exact value.

#### occupancy(u, v)

Foreground indicator at model coordinates `(u, v)`.

`u` and `v` are float arrays of any matching shape. Returns an array of the
same shape, boolean or float in `[0, 1]`. Points outside [`extent`](_autosummary/inkmap.models.base.html.md#inkmap.models.base.Model.extent) must
return 0 – callers rely on that to bound the mark.

Must be vectorised: it is called with millions of points.

* **Return type:**
  `ndarray`

Rasterise any model to a float `[0, 1]` array at `scale` px per model unit.

# _autosummary/inkmap.models.freeform.html.md

# inkmap.models.freeform

Models for shapes that are not on a grid: rasters, polygons, and text.

These are the escape hatches. Anything you can draw, scan, or describe as outlines
becomes a model here, and the rest of the package treats it exactly like a QR symbol.

[`PolygonModel`](_autosummary/inkmap.models.freeform.html.md#inkmap.models.freeform.PolygonModel) is the only *exact* one – a point-in-polygon test has no
resolution. [`RasterModel`](_autosummary/inkmap.models.freeform.html.md#inkmap.models.freeform.RasterModel) quantises to its own grid, so give it enough
resolution: its cells should be several times smaller than an image pixel maps to,
or the raster’s own edges become the accuracy limit rather than the photograph’s.

### Functions

| [`text_model`](_autosummary/inkmap.models.freeform.html.md#inkmap.models.freeform.text_model)(text, \*\*kwargs)   | Convenience constructor for [`GlyphModel`](_autosummary/inkmap.models.freeform.html.md#inkmap.models.freeform.GlyphModel).   |
|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|

### Classes

| [`RasterModel`](_autosummary/inkmap.models.freeform.html.md#inkmap.models.freeform.RasterModel)(mask[, metadata])                  | Foreground given as an image: a logo, a scan, a pre-rendered glyph.   |
|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`PolygonModel`](_autosummary/inkmap.models.freeform.html.md#inkmap.models.freeform.PolygonModel)(polygons[, extent_override, ...]) | Foreground as closed outlines, with holes -- the exact case.          |
| [`GlyphModel`](_autosummary/inkmap.models.freeform.html.md#inkmap.models.freeform.GlyphModel)(text[, font_path, font_size, ...])  | A run of printed text, rendered once at high resolution.              |

### *class* inkmap.models.freeform.GlyphModel(text, font_path=None, font_size=256, padding=8, metadata=dict())

Bases: [`BaseModel`](_autosummary/inkmap.models.base.html.md#inkmap.models.base.BaseModel)

A run of printed text, rendered once at high resolution.

Text is a raster problem in practice: fonts are outlines, but hinting, kerning and
anti-aliasing mean the printed shape is what the renderer produced, not the ideal
outline. So this renders through PIL at a resolution well above the photograph’s
and treats the result as a [`RasterModel`](_autosummary/inkmap.models.freeform.html.md#inkmap.models.freeform.RasterModel).

Requires Pillow, and a font file for anything but the (very coarse) PIL default –
pass `font_path`. Model space is the rendered pixel grid.

#### *property* feature_size *: [float](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)*

Typical stroke width of the rendered text, in raster cells.

### *class* inkmap.models.freeform.PolygonModel(polygons, extent_override=None, metadata=dict())

Bases: [`BaseModel`](_autosummary/inkmap.models.base.html.md#inkmap.models.base.BaseModel)

Foreground as closed outlines, with holes – the exact case.

`polygons` is a sequence of `(N, 2)` float arrays of `(u, v)` vertices. Use
the even-odd rule: a polygon inside another cuts a hole, which is what letters like
‘o’ and ‘B’ need. No resolution is involved, so coverage error is limited only by
the supersampling rate.

#### occupancy(u, v)

Even-odd crossing test, vectorised over all points and all edges.

* **Return type:**
  `ndarray`

### *class* inkmap.models.freeform.RasterModel(mask, metadata=dict())

Bases: [`BaseModel`](_autosummary/inkmap.models.base.html.md#inkmap.models.base.BaseModel)

Foreground given as an image: a logo, a scan, a pre-rendered glyph.

`mask` may be boolean or float in `[0, 1]`; float is respected, so an
anti-aliased source keeps its soft edges. Model space is `(width, height)` in
raster cells.

### inkmap.models.freeform.text_model(text, \*\*kwargs)

Convenience constructor for [`GlyphModel`](_autosummary/inkmap.models.freeform.html.md#inkmap.models.freeform.GlyphModel).

* **Return type:**
  [`GlyphModel`](_autosummary/inkmap.models.freeform.html.md#inkmap.models.freeform.GlyphModel)


# _autosummary/inkmap.models.grid.html.md

# inkmap.models.grid

Models whose foreground is defined on a regular grid: QR symbols and barcodes.

Both answer occupancy by indexing, so their coverage is exact up to the supersampling
rate – there is no intermediate bitmap to quantise them twice.

### Classes

| [`MatrixModel`](_autosummary/inkmap.models.grid.html.md#inkmap.models.grid.MatrixModel)(cells[, metadata])      | A 2-D grid of foreground/background cells -- a QR symbol's module matrix.         |
|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`BarsModel`](_autosummary/inkmap.models.grid.html.md#inkmap.models.grid.BarsModel)(bars[, height, metadata]) | A 1-D run of foreground/background bars, extruded vertically -- a linear barcode. |

### *class* inkmap.models.grid.BarsModel(bars, height=20.0, metadata=dict())

Bases: [`BaseModel`](_autosummary/inkmap.models.base.html.md#inkmap.models.base.BaseModel)

A 1-D run of foreground/background bars, extruded vertically – a linear barcode.

`bars` is a boolean array over the narrowest module width, `True` for a bar.
Model space is `(len(bars), height)`; `height` is in the same module units, so
a 95-module EAN-13 printed twice as tall as it is wide would use `height=190`.
Height rarely matters for coverage (the pattern is constant along `v`) but it
fixes the aspect ratio for rendering and refinement.

#### *property* feature_size *: [float](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)*

One module – the narrowest bar, which is what must be resolved.

### *class* inkmap.models.grid.MatrixModel(cells, metadata=dict())

Bases: [`BaseModel`](_autosummary/inkmap.models.base.html.md#inkmap.models.base.BaseModel)

A 2-D grid of foreground/background cells – a QR symbol’s module matrix.

`cells[row, col]` is `True` where the cell is foreground. Model space is
`(n_cols, n_rows)` in cells, origin at the mark’s own top-left, so cell
`(i, j)` occupies `u in [j, j+1)`, `v in [i, i+1)`.

Also serves Data Matrix, Aztec, and any other matrix symbology: only the cell
grid matters here, not how it was decoded.

#### *property* feature_size *: [float](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)*

One cell – for a matrix symbology the cell *is* the smallest feature.


# _autosummary/inkmap.models.html.md

# inkmap.models

Shape models: what the foreground is expected to look like.

A model is anything that can answer [`occupancy()`](_autosummary/inkmap.models.base.html.md#inkmap.models.base.Model.occupancy) – is
this point in the mark’s own coordinate system foreground? – plus report its
[`extent`](_autosummary/inkmap.models.base.html.md#inkmap.models.base.Model.extent). That is the whole contract, and it is what
lets one pipeline serve QR symbols, barcodes, printed letters and arbitrary artwork.

> from inkmap import models

> models.MatrixModel(cells)          # QR, Data Matrix, Aztec: a grid of cells
> models.BarsModel(bars)             # EAN, Code 128, …: a run of bars
> models.RasterModel(mask)           # a logo, a scan, anything you can draw
> models.PolygonModel(outlines)      # exact vector outlines, holes included
> models.GlyphModel(“ABC”)           # printed text, rendered via Pillow

Anything duck-typed to the same two members works just as well – there is no base
class to inherit and no registration step.

### Functions

| [`render_model`](_autosummary/inkmap.models.html.md#inkmap.models.render_model)(model[, scale, supersample])   | Rasterise any model to a float `[0, 1]` array at `scale` px per model unit.              |
|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`text_model`](_autosummary/inkmap.models.html.md#inkmap.models.text_model)(text, \*\*kwargs)                | Convenience constructor for [`GlyphModel`](_autosummary/inkmap.models.html.md#inkmap.models.GlyphModel). |

### Classes

| [`Model`](_autosummary/inkmap.models.html.md#inkmap.models.Model)(\*args, \*\*kwargs)                      | The shape of a mark, in its own coordinate system.                                |
|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`BaseModel`](_autosummary/inkmap.models.html.md#inkmap.models.BaseModel)()                                    | Mixin supplying `render()` and a `feature_size` estimate.                         |
| [`MatrixModel`](_autosummary/inkmap.models.html.md#inkmap.models.MatrixModel)(cells[, metadata])                 | A 2-D grid of foreground/background cells -- a QR symbol's module matrix.         |
| [`BarsModel`](_autosummary/inkmap.models.html.md#inkmap.models.BarsModel)(bars[, height, metadata])            | A 1-D run of foreground/background bars, extruded vertically -- a linear barcode. |
| [`RasterModel`](_autosummary/inkmap.models.html.md#inkmap.models.RasterModel)(mask[, metadata])                  | Foreground given as an image: a logo, a scan, a pre-rendered glyph.               |
| [`PolygonModel`](_autosummary/inkmap.models.html.md#inkmap.models.PolygonModel)(polygons[, extent_override, ...]) | Foreground as closed outlines, with holes -- the exact case.                      |
| [`GlyphModel`](_autosummary/inkmap.models.html.md#inkmap.models.GlyphModel)(text[, font_path, font_size, ...])  | A run of printed text, rendered once at high resolution.                          |

### *class* inkmap.models.BarsModel(bars, height=20.0, metadata=dict())

Bases: [`BaseModel`](_autosummary/inkmap.models.base.html.md#inkmap.models.base.BaseModel)

A 1-D run of foreground/background bars, extruded vertically – a linear barcode.

`bars` is a boolean array over the narrowest module width, `True` for a bar.
Model space is `(len(bars), height)`; `height` is in the same module units, so

Height rarely matters for coverage (the pattern is constant along `v`) but it

#### *property* feature_size *: [float](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)*

### *class* inkmap.models.BaseModel

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

Mixin supplying [`render()`](_autosummary/inkmap.models.html.md#inkmap.models.BaseModel.render) and a [`feature_size`](_autosummary/inkmap.models.html.md#inkmap.models.BaseModel.feature_size) estimate.

Anything with `extent` and `occupancy` gets both for free.

#### *property* feature_size *: [float](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)*

Estimated smallest-feature size, in model units, from the rendered shape.

Taken as twice the median distance-to-edge over foreground – i.e. the typical
stroke width. The median rather than the minimum, because every shape has a few
pixels at a corner or a serif whose distance-to-edge is near zero, and letting
those set the scale would declare every image unmeasurable.

Cached: it costs a render, and the answer cannot change for an immutable model.

#### render(scale=8.0, , supersample=4)

Rasterise the model at `scale` pixels per model unit.

Returns a float array in `[0, 1]` where 1 is foreground. Anti-aliased by
supersampling, because the main consumer is template alignment against a
photograph, and a hard-edged template correlates poorly with soft real edges.

* **Return type:**
  `ndarray`
